title: Taiwan is investigating 17 Chinese firms for poaching its chip talent
excerpt: Taiwan’s Investigation Bureau has searched 64 sites and questioned 114 people in a probe of 17 Chinese firms accused of illegally recruiting semiconductor talent.
content_html:
Taiwan is again accusing China of trying to buy the talent it cannot build. The island’s Investigation Bureau said it is probing 17 Chinese companies suspected of illegally recruiting local high-tech engineers.

The sweep was substantial. Between mid-July and early August, investigators searched 64 locations and questioned 114 people, in one of the larger actions since the bureau set up a dedicated task force for this work.

The alleged playbook is familiar. According to the bureau, Chinese firms disguise themselves as Taiwanese or foreign-funded businesses, open unauthorised offices, or work through staffing agencies to hide who is really doing the hiring.

The targets are precise. The companies under scrutiny cluster around semiconductor manufacturing and integrated-circuit design, the two fields where Taiwan’s lead is most valuable and hardest for Beijing to replicate on its own.

The named firms span the island. They include Actions Technology in Taipei and chip-tool and materials suppliers across New Taipei, Taoyuan and Tainan, several of which operate in the equipment niches that export controls have made hardest for China to source.

That is the wider context. Cut off from the most advanced tools and chips by US-led restrictions, Beijing has leaned harder on the one input that sanctions cannot easily block, which is the people who know how to build them.

Taiwan treats this as a security matter, not a hiring dispute. Poaching a senior process engineer can transfer years of accumulated know-how in a single contract, and the government has moved to make such recruitment a legal risk rather than a quiet career move.

The effort is not new. The task force behind these searches was created in 2020 and has looked into more than 100 cases since, a running campaign that flares into public view each time a fresh batch of raids is announced.

Taiwan has tightened the rules to match. It bars Chinese companies from operating on the island without approval and restricts locals from working for them, giving prosecutors a legal basis to treat concealed recruitment as an offence rather than ordinary competition.

The value of a single hire is easy to underestimate. A veteran process engineer carries the hard-won detail of how a leading-edge production line actually runs, the kind of knowledge that never appears in a patent filing and takes rivals years to reconstruct.

The stakes sit at the centre of the chip war. Taiwan’s dominance is so strategically sensitive that ASML is reported to be able to disable its machines on the island should China ever invade, a measure of how much the world’s advanced computing rests there.

Cut off from that hardware, China has been improvising. Firms such as DeepSeek are designing their own AI chips to route around US curbs, and the whole effort depends on engineers who understand advanced fabrication.

Domestic champions are pushing too. Huawei’s research arm, led by its so-called chip queen, is chasing new methods to squeeze more from the tools China can still get, another sign of how much rides on talent.

Beijing rejects the framing. It casts cross-strait hiring as a normal flow of talent and accuses Taipei of politicising ordinary recruitment, a dispute that mirrors the two sides’ deeper disagreement over the island’s status.

None of the accused firms has been convicted, and the investigation is ongoing. But the pattern is by now well worn, and each round of searches underlines how thin the human margin behind Taiwan’s advantage really is.

For Taipei, that is the uncomfortable lesson. The island can guard its factories and its machines, yet the knowledge lives in people, and people can always be offered a better deal across the strait.

content_html_zh:
台湾再次指责中国试图购买其无法培养的人才。 岛内调查局表示，正在调查17家涉嫌非法招聘当地高科技工程师的中国公司。

这次扫荡是巨大的。 7月中旬至8月初，调查人员搜查了64个地点，询问了114人，这是该局成立专门工作组开展这项工作以来规模较大的行动之一。

所谓的剧本很熟悉。 据该局称，中国企业将自己伪装成台资或外资企业，开设未经授权的办事处，或通过人才中介机构隐藏真正在招聘的人。

目标是精确的。 受到审查的公司主要集中在半导体制造和集成电路设计领域，台湾的领先地位在这两个领域最有价值，也最难被北京复制。

这些被点名的公司遍布全岛。 其中包括台北的珠海炬力科技有限公司，以及新北、桃园和台南的芯片工具和材料供应商，其中一些供应商从事出口管制导致中国最难采购的设备领域。

这是更广泛的背景。 由于美国主导的限制措施，北京无法获得最先进的工具和芯片，因此更加依赖制裁无法轻易阻止的一项投入，即知道如何制造这些工具和芯片的人。

台湾将此视为安全问题，而不是雇佣纠纷。 挖走一名高级工艺工程师可以通过一份合同转让多年积累的专业知识，而政府已经采取行动，使这种招聘成为一种法律风险，而不是一种悄然的职业变动。

这种努力并不新鲜。 这些搜查背后的特别工作组成立于 2020 年，此后已调查了 100 多起案件，每次宣布新一批搜查行动时，这项持续开展的活动就会引起公众的注意。

台湾也收紧了规则来配合。 它禁止中国公司未经批准在岛上开展业务，并限制当地人为他们工作，这为检察官将隐匿招聘视为犯罪行为而非普通竞争行为提供了法律依据。

单一雇佣的价值很容易被低估。 一位经验丰富的工艺工程师掌握了前沿生产线实际运行方式的来之不易的细节，这种知识从未出现在专利申请中，并且需要竞争对手花费数年时间才能重建。

赌注处于芯片战争的中心。 台湾的主导地位在战略上非常敏感，据报道，如果中国入侵，ASML 能够禁用其在台湾的机器，这衡量了那里有多少世界先进计算技术。

与这些硬件隔绝后，中国一直在即兴发挥。 DeepSeek 等公司正在设计自己的人工智能芯片，以绕过美国的限制，而整个努力取决于了解先进制造的工程师。

国内冠军也在努力。 华为的研究部门在其所谓的“芯片女王”的领导下，正在寻求新的方法，以从中国仍然可以获得的工具中榨取更多的资源，这是人才在多大程度上发挥作用的另一个迹象。

北京拒绝接受这一框架。 它将两岸招聘视为正常的人才流动，并指责台北将普通招聘政治化，这一争端反映了两岸在台湾地位问题上更深层次的分歧。

没有一家被指控的公司被定罪，调查正在进行中。 但这种模式现在已经很陈旧了，每一轮搜索都突显出台湾优势背后的人力优势是多么微弱。

对于台北来说，这是一个令人不安的教训。 岛屿可以保护它的工厂和机器，但知识存在于人们之中，而且海峡对岸的人们总是可以得到更好的待遇。
